lab.name: CDS Eval Lab
lab.tagline: I measure whether clinical AI is actually safe to deploy.

scope.blurb: The harness covers both single-turn lookups (one prompt, one answer, one score) and multi-turn dialogue (parent vignettes, clinician follow-ups, conversation budgets). Different failure modes, different rubrics — measured separately so a system can't trade one for the other.

workstreams.title: Clinical decision support
workstreams.tagline: Single-turn lookups, primary care and pediatrics.
workstreams.blurb: Hand-curated query suites stress-testing what frontier LLMs and specialist CDS APIs do at the point of care. The deep-dive that runs the length of this page.

workstreams.title: Pediatric triage assistant
workstreams.tagline: Modular evaluation of a parent-facing AI system.
workstreams.blurb: Four capability modules (onboarding, communication patterns, parenting support, medical triage) scored by 4 specialized judges across 5–8 gates each. Six prompt iterations, sixteen parent personas, three hundred and seventy-nine scored conversations.

workstreams.title: Conversational health agent
workstreams.tagline: Multi-turn dialogue evaluation for chronic disease management.
workstreams.blurb: Synthetic patient simulator running multi-turn conversations (up to 25 turns each) against an adult chronic-disease health agent. Forty personas including twenty adversarial archetypes (skepticism, avoidance, anxiety, tech aversion).

ws_peds.system_description: Parent-facing pediatric triage assistant. Conversations happen in lay language with caregivers — symptoms, behavior questions, developmental concerns — and the system has to land on a safe disposition (home / urgent / ER) without sounding clinical. The harness composes a base prompt with one capability module per evaluation run, so a regression in one capability can be located without re-testing the others.

architecture.intro: The framework, not just the scenarios, is the work.

rows.label: Modular prompts
rows.value: 5 components (base + 4 capability modules) composed at runtime per evaluation cell

rows.label: Specialized judges
rows.value: 4 module-specific judge prompts, each with its own 5–8-gate rubric

rows.label: Parent personas
rows.value: 16 archetypes varying medical literacy, anxiety, communication style, health-seeking behavior

rows.label: Prompt iterations
rows.value: P1 → P7 over six months, each iteration targeting a specific gate failure

rows.label: Variance testing
rows.value: Each red-flag scenario run twice with random personas to surface prompt brittleness

modules.name: Onboarding
modules.purpose: Collect child info, calculate age correctly, never assume.

modules.name: Communication patterns
modules.purpose: Match the parent's register, ask one question at a time, avoid robotic clinician-speak.

modules.name: Parenting support
modules.purpose: Validate before solving. Normalize developmentally. Escalate when an apparent parenting question is actually a medical one.

modules.name: Medical triage
modules.purpose: Red-flag recognition, disposition accuracy, and scope discipline. The safety floor of the entire system, decomposed into eight discrete decision points.

findings.headline: Red-flag recognition: 100% accuracy on the twelve critical scenarios.
findings.body: Across breathing emergency, neonatal fever, meningococcemia, anaphylaxis, cardiac failure, and seven others — twelve of twelve correctly identified. The clinical reasoning is solid. The failures live elsewhere.

findings.headline: Variance as signal: a third of red-flag runs flipped between PASS and FAIL.
findings.body: Re-running each red-flag scenario with a different parent persona surfaced inconsistency the single-pass score could not see. Four of twelve scenarios flipped — a 33% variance rate. Reliability isn't an aggregate score, it's whether the system holds up when the conversation goes a different direction.

findings.headline: Every variance case had the same root cause: scope drift after escalation.
findings.body: Gate 7 (scope boundary) failures in 100% of the variance scenarios. The assistant promised post-hospital follow-up ("I'll check in with you tomorrow") outside its triage scope. Gate 8 (conversation closure) failures in 75% — fifteen-plus exchanges continuing after the parent was already in the ambulance. Pure prompt-level discipline problems, not clinical-reasoning failures.

findings.headline: Parenting support cleared every gate.
findings.body: Recent sample: 100% pass across validation, developmental normalization, parent-expertise respect, escalation, and identifying the real need. One scored conversation about oppositional behavior correctly identified parental burnout as the root cause and committed to follow-up — exactly what a human clinician would have done.

findings.headline: Disposition accuracy ~85%; clinical judgment is rarely the failure mode.
findings.body: When the system errs on disposition it's typically a protocol-mismatch deviation that a clinician would defend, not a misread of the clinical picture. Surfacing this required the gate decomposition: an aggregate quality score smoothed over the difference between "wrong clinically" and "reasonable deviation."

findings.headline: Decomposing the judge mattered as much as decomposing the prompt.
findings.body: Splitting the monolithic Claude-as-judge rubric into four specialized judges (one per module) sharpened the criteria language and made the gate failures legible. The framework is now the artifact, not just the scenarios — modular prompts, specialized judges, persona-driven robustness testing all reusable for any composed-prompt system.

ws_conv.system_description: Adult chronic-disease conversational health agent — type-2 diabetes, obesity, hypertension, GERD. Patients ask in their own words, multi-turn, with all the usual real-life noise (interruptions, partial information, contradictions, denial).

simulator.title: The agent conversation simulator
simulator.body: A frontier LLM plays the patient. The agent under test plays itself. Conversations are scripted only by persona profile (history, motivation, communication style, adversarial archetype if any) and run for up to twenty-five turns. Each conversation is scored on partnership quality, red-flag handling, constraint acknowledgement, and continuity across turns.

personas.intro: Forty personas. Twenty are standard archetypes (newly diagnosed, well-managed, transitioning meds, peri-procedural). Twenty are adversarial archetypes built to stress specific failure modes.

archetypes.label: The skeptic
archetypes.tests: Does the agent earn trust without being defensive?

archetypes.label: The avoider
archetypes.tests: Does the agent name the elephant in the room?

archetypes.label: The anxious patient
archetypes.tests: Does the agent reassure without dismissing?

archetypes.label: The tech-averse
archetypes.tests: Does the agent meet the patient where they are technologically?

findings.headline: Average conversation depth was eighteen turns.
findings.body: Across twenty-five completed conversations in a recent full run, the agent sustained engagement well past the point where most lookup-style evals stop measuring. Single-turn benchmarks would have scored this system favorably and entirely missed the dimensions where it shines.

findings.headline: Adversarial personas are the cheapest signal.
findings.body: The twenty adversarial archetypes (skeptic, avoider, anxious, tech-averse) surfaced more distinct failure modes than the twenty standard personas combined. The pattern from CDS work holds: hand-curated adversarial cases differentiate better than larger but uniform sets.

findings.headline: Multi-turn surfaces failure modes lookup cannot.
findings.body: Personality consistency, memory of earlier disclosures, willingness to revisit a previous turn — these only show up over a sustained dialogue. A lookup-style harness would not have flagged the failures the simulator caught.

suites.name: Golden — Primary care core
suites.purpose: Hand-curated ambulatory lookups across 23 domains. The floor every CDS system must clear — and unlike the public benchmarks, it does not saturate at the top.
suites.scored_by: Frontier LLM judge, dual rubric (full CDS + content-only).

suites.name: Freshness — Guidelines that moved
suites.purpose: Questions whose correct answer changed in 2024–2026. Detects models living in 2023.
suites.scored_by: Old-answer vs new-answer binary + partial-credit rubric.

suites.name: Hallucination — Clinical traps
suites.purpose: Contraindications, dangerous dosing, false-premise queries. The model must push back.
suites.scored_by: Pass/fail by trap category, judged on whether the trap was caught.

suites.name: HalluHard — Fabricated entities
suites.purpose: Invented trial names, fake scoring systems, plausible-sounding nonsense. Tests refusal vs confabulation. Methodology adapted from the HalluHard paper (arXiv 2602.01031, 2026).
suites.scored_by: PASS / PARTIAL / FAIL by graded refusal quality.

suites.name: Edge — Pediatric rare disease
suites.purpose: Wilson disease, inborn errors of metabolism, atypical presentations. Tests parametric depth past the top-100 conditions.

suites.name: PC-136 — Primary-care professional
suites.purpose: Run paper-faithful from HealthBench Pro (OpenAI, April 2026) — same grader, same length-adjustment formula. The external-validity check on the rest of the harness.
suites.scored_by: Reference-rubric scoring; length-adjusted ×100 per paper methodology.

suites.name: Peds Dosing — Mg/kg and contraindications
suites.purpose: Six categories built to catch dose-correctness failures: 1:1000 vs 1:10,000 epinephrine, ceftriaxone in a neonate, ibuprofen under six months, hypotonic IVF, adult-dose oseltamivir in an infant.
suites.scored_by: Per-category pass/fail by a physician-authored rubric.

leaderboard.notes: Best clinical content overall. Citations are the weakness.
Strong citations, bimodal quality. 18 critical errors flagged — vendor notified.
Top of stack on every clinical-quality bench. Slowest and priciest.
Lean tuned CDS prompt (~2.8K chars). Closes a 17-point gap to specialist APIs at ~6× lower cost.
Heavier parallel-reason variant. Buys 3–4 points on every dimension at ~3× the cost.
Strong floor, but raw is not CDS-ready. Misses contraindications it would catch with a prompt.
Cheaper and faster, but more confident wrong answers than its peer.
Beats one frontier model on the Hard subset. Runs on a workstation. Zero PHI exposure.
Too eager to please. Fails the hallucination suites badly.

timeline.title: Wired the first three sources
timeline.body: Built clients for a specialist MCP integration, a specialist text API, and a web-search pipeline. The first surprise arrived early: loading specialist articles as RAG context made a frontier model six points worse. The reference tool was acting as a noise injector.

timeline.title: Hand-curated the Golden 60
timeline.body: Sixty queries across 23 ambulatory domains, written by hand. Built the three internal suites — Golden, Freshness, Hallucination — that still anchor the harness today. Hand-curated traps surface failure modes no commercial benchmark catches because no commercial benchmark is allowed to be adversarial.

timeline.title: Sixteen rounds at ~85, then a seventeen-point lift on a single rewrite
timeline.body: Sixteen numbered prompt iterations all sat within ±1.5 points of each other. The breakthrough was structural: a template that required explicit guideline-version citation and a fixed clinical section order. It lifted every frontier model 17–20 points and zeroed out hallucination fails. The prompt is the largest single lever in the stack.

timeline.title: When a 29-point variance became 6
timeline.body: One trap query had been swinging 29 points between identical judge calls at temperature 1.0. Switching to median-of-three at temperature 0.3, with anti-anchoring and date-awareness in the prompt, dropped the spread to 0–6 points on the same input.

timeline.title: A blinded physician review inverted the leaderboard
timeline.body: Ten queries, four systems, blind ranking. The prompt-tuned frontier model the automated judge had ranked at the top won zero. The discrepancy was freshness — fluent answers built on last year's guidelines, indistinguishable from current ones to a non-date-aware judge.

timeline.title: Designed a query-decontextualization layer
timeline.body: A small model decontextualizes the clinical query before it leaves the local environment; the CDS endpoint only sees the abstracted version. Validated against 132 adversarial PHI stress tests, 131 passing. Closes the BAA gap for vendors that won't sign one — and a side effect of appending currency terms to every search lifted Freshness from 1.5 to 2.0.

timeline.title: Hand-curated query sets caught what off-the-shelf benchmarks couldn't
timeline.body: Off-the-shelf benchmarks measure general competence; they don't surface the failure modes that hurt my patients. The thirty hand-curated false-premise traps cost a few hours to write and surfaced more clinically-meaningful failures than every commercial bench combined. The work shifted from running other people's benchmarks to building my own.

timeline.phase: 08 · Cost-opt with local models — didn't work
timeline.title: Six local-model candidates, no winner for production
timeline.body: Open-weights 27B held its own on Golden (88.8) but failed Freshness at 0.93/2 — parametric staleness no prompt can fix — and gave dangerous answers on the hallucination traps. The cleaner finding from the same exercise: cost-optimizing the system under test is the wrong axis. Swapping the judge for a calibrated cheap model cut total eval spend ~15× without changing the leaderboard.

timeline.title: Pediatric suites running throughout, not bolted on at the end
timeline.body: Peds dosing traps (1:1,000 vs 1:10,000 epinephrine, ibuprofen under six months, hypotonic IVF), peds freshness probes anchored to 2024–26 AAP/AHA shifts, and a peds hallucination set focused on fabricated criteria. Pediatrics is where the rare diseases live, where the dose-by-weight rules bite, and where my patients are.

timeline_meta.framing: Four moments did the most work: the prompt rewrite (03), the judge fix (04), the physician 0/10 (05), and the shift from running benchmarks to curating them (07). Every other finding sits downstream of one of those four.

example_queries.description: A beta-lactam allergy paired with a request for a beta-lactam. The system must refuse to dose and surface the cross-reactivity risk.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Models that pattern-match 'strep throat' → first-line antibiotic without re-reading the allergy field.

example_queries.description: Antipyretic dosing for a neonate. The clinically correct response is age-based: acetaminophen has narrow indications under three months and ibuprofen is contraindicated under six months. The right answer is a workup pathway, not a mg/kg number.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Models that answer the question as asked instead of pushing back on the premise.

example_queries.description: A vaccine schedule item that changed in the last 12 months. Old answer is wrong; new answer is in the most recent ACIP update.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Parametric staleness. Models without retrieval or with stale retrieval still confidently give the old answer.

example_queries.description: Asks about a trial with a plausible-sounding name that does not exist. The system must refuse instead of confabulating findings.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Models that generate fluent fake methodology and results. The query is intentionally invented.

example_queries.description: Borderline lab value in a high-risk patient framed as a reassurance request. The right answer challenges the framing.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Models that mirror the parent's framing instead of escalating risk.

example_queries.description: Pediatric inborn error of metabolism presenting with a common chief complaint. Tests depth past the top-100 conditions.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Systems trained heavily on adult primary care that thin out at the long tail.

example_queries.description: Asks for the epinephrine dose in an anaphylaxis scenario. The 1:1,000 (IM) vs 1:10,000 (IV) distinction is the difference between an appropriate dose and the wrong route entirely.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Models that recall the number without locking the concentration. Frontier models still miss this without a prompt that forces them to name the concentration first.

example_queries.description: RSV prophylaxis for the 2025–26 season. Nirsevimab is now the AAP-preferred agent for most infants in their first RSV season; palivizumab is reserved for narrow high-risk groups when nirsevimab is not available.
example_queries.what_it_catches: Models that confidently quote the pre-2023 palivizumab-first algorithm as the default.

findings.headline: The system prompt is the largest single lever.
findings.body: Going from a raw frontier model to the same model with a tuned CDS prompt is +17 to +20 points on the Golden suite. Cross-model differences within the same prompt are 1 to 3 points. Most of the perceived 'specialist CDS API' moat is actually a prompting moat.

findings.headline: Specialist APIs are not safer. They fail differently.
findings.body: One specialist endpoint had 18 errors across 60 queries — outdated screening thresholds and contradicted treatments stated with high confidence. Specialist branding does not substitute for an evaluation harness.

findings.headline: One web search is the best dollar you'll spend.
findings.body: Zero searches to one search lifts Freshness by +0.40 and Edge by +7 points. The first search is not fixing knowledge gaps — it's fixing currency and depth on hard cases. Going from one to five searches buys nothing on quality and adds hallucination failures.

findings.headline: More retrieval lowers resistance to fabricated user premises.
findings.body: Counter-intuitively, more searches mean the model becomes more confident it has evidence — and more willing to play along with a false premise in the question. The 0-hallucination configurations on the trap suite use one search or none.

findings.headline: A local 27B model beats one frontier model on the Hard subset.
findings.body: Open-weights 27B running on a workstation hit 88.8 on Golden and 77% on the hallucination traps — outperforming one of the two frontier APIs at zero marginal cost and zero PHI exposure. The bottleneck shifted from 'does the model exist' to 'is the prompt right.'

findings.headline: Most 'hallucination' is actually agreeableness.
findings.body: The 4B model failed 20 of 30 trap queries not because it lacked knowledge, but because it accepted false premises from the prompt. Models that refuse to disagree with the user are dangerous in CDS regardless of their parametric depth.

findings.headline: Citation strength does not predict content quality.
findings.body: The system with the strongest literature citations had the highest critical-error rate. Citations are a packaging dimension, not a quality signal. They must be scored separately or they bias the rubric.

findings.headline: Cheap judges are good enough — if you calibrate them.
findings.body: A small frontier judge model hit MAE 5.65 vs the gold-standard judge with r=0.77 rank-order correlation. Running graders on a $0.20-per-million model instead of a $3 model cut evaluation cost ~15× without changing the leaderboard order.

findings.headline: Length-adjustment compresses the score gap between vendors.
findings.body: Verbose responses score higher on rubric-based judges by accidentally hitting more bullet points. Once length is held constant, the per-query gap between a tuned frontier model and a specialist API closes to 1–3 points on the public PC-136 set.

findings.headline: Hand-curated traps caught what every commercial bench missed.
findings.body: The 30 false-premise queries were the cheapest safety signal in the project — a few hours of physician time, more failure modes surfaced than HealthBench Pro, golden_60, and edge_15 combined.

findings.headline: The score depends on the rubric, not the model.
findings.body: The same response from one of the systems we evaluated scored 92 on an internal clinical-quality rubric and 26 on a length-adjusted public benchmark. A 65-point gap on identical text. Any CDS leaderboard that doesn't publish the rubric alongside the number is not actually interpretable.

findings.headline: Within-family judges agree better than cross-vendor ones.
findings.body: Six cheap-judge candidates from four model families. The only one that tracked the production reference judge was the small model from the same family. Cross-vendor candidates at the same price tier clustered near r=0.2 — wrong consistently, which is uncorrectable. Pick judges from the reference family, not just the cheaper price point.

findings.headline: Coefficient of variation is the safety signal, not the mean.
findings.body: Two specialist APIs had similar headline scores but stdev 7 vs stdev 21. The lower-mean system was the safer system because its worst-case answer was 56/100; the higher-mean system's worst-case was 1/100. 'Consistent good' beats 'occasionally great with catastrophic floors' every time in clinical use.

methodology_contributions.title: Dual-rubric scoring across registers
methodology_contributions.body: Same clinical condition, scored twice: once on a parent-vignette rubric (lay-language narrative, family-counseling criteria) and once on a clinician-query rubric (focused workup, dose-correctness, citation accuracy). A representative response landed at 95% on one rubric and 69% on the other — pure methodology artifact. A real CDS tool serves both registers; single-axis evaluation under-measures.

methodology_contributions.title: The judge calibration protocol
methodology_contributions.body: Median-of-three calls at temperature 0.3, with anti-anchoring instructions and date-awareness baked into the prompt. New candidate judges run against a 20-case × 3-run calibration set vs the reference judge; MAE and Pearson r on rank-order both tracked. Across four candidate judges on 62 criteria, inter-judge agreement hit 93.5% — a floor worth measuring before publishing any single-judge score.

methodology_contributions.title: The blinded-comparator design
methodology_contributions.body: When publishing comparisons that include both an open tool and a commercial system, name the open default and blind the commercial alternatives as Source A / Source B / etc. Brand recognition shouldn't tilt the comparison; the right choice is the one that fits the workflow. A middle path between 'name everyone' (commercially loaded) and 'blind everyone' (uninterpretable).

methodology_contributions.title: Adversarial freshness + hallucination as the cheapest safety signal
methodology_contributions.body: Hand-built two adversarial suites: thirty guideline-changed-in-the-last-twelve-months freshness probes with old-answer/new-answer ground truth, and thirty false-premise traps that bait fabricated citations. A few hours each to build. More failure modes surfaced than the largest commercial bench combined.

methodology_contributions.title: Modular composition with specialized judges
methodology_contributions.body: Compose the system prompt from a base plus one capability module per evaluation run; score each cell with a judge specialized to that module's rubric. When a capability regresses, the gate analysis points at it directly instead of disappearing into a global mean. The framework is the artifact — reusable for any composed-prompt system whose behavior emerges from interaction between parts.

methodology_contributions.title: Variance-as-signal
methodology_contributions.body: Re-run each high-stakes scenario with different personas instead of trusting a single pass. On the pediatric triage harness this surfaced a 33% flip rate on red-flag scenarios that the aggregate pass-rate completely hid. Brittleness becomes a measurable property of the prompt, not a hunch — and the root cause (scope-boundary drift after escalation) was named precisely because variance pointed at the gate that was flipping.

methodology_contributions.title: Adversarial-archetype personas
methodology_contributions.body: For conversational AI, the persona library is the brand. Name the failure mode first — skeptic, avoider, anxious patient, tech-averse — then build a persona designed to stress that mode across a multi-turn dialogue. Twenty adversarial archetypes surfaced more distinct failure modes than the twenty standard ones combined. Same pattern as adversarial single-turn traps, applied to dialogue.

economics.intro: Three months of evaluation cost about one thousand dollars across roughly three hundred and thirty million tokens. The line items are not where most teams assume.

rows.label: Judge model calls (grading)
rows.note: Every response scored by 1–2 judges across 6 suites adds up fast.

rows.label: System-under-test calls (the LLMs being measured)
rows.note: Most of the systems being tested are cheap. The verbose ones are not.

rows.label: Specialist CDS API calls
rows.note: Per-query pricing dominates if you score a full suite against them.

economics.punchline: Cost-optimizing the system under test is the wrong axis. Cost-optimizing the judge is where the savings live.

methodology.title: Dual-rubric scoring
methodology.body: Every response is scored twice: once on the full production rubric (accuracy + completeness + specificity + citations + format) and once on content-only (drop citations + format penalties). The gap between the two tells you whether a system is losing on substance or on packaging.

methodology.title: Judge calibration
methodology.body: Judges are themselves evaluated. Each candidate judge is run against a small set scored by a frontier reference judge. Mean absolute error and Pearson r on rank-order both matter — a low MAE with low r means the cheap judge is wrong consistently, which is uncorrectable. The current production judge holds MAE 5.65 with r=0.77 vs the reference.

methodology.title: HIPAA-safe query decontextualization
methodology.body: Queries containing PHI are routed through a small model that strips identifiers and re-expresses the clinical question before the prompt ever leaves the local environment. The CDS endpoint sees only the abstracted question. Decontextualization quality is itself benchmarked on >1,000 sample queries.

methodology.title: Length-adjusted scoring
methodology.body: Longer answers tend to score higher on completeness regardless of content. Wherever raw length is reward-hackable, scores are normalized to a length-adjusted variant so verbosity does not buy a system its way up the table. PC-136 uses the HealthBench Pro length-adjustment formula directly.

methodology.title: Single-turn scope
methodology.body: This site reports single-turn results only — one prompt, one answer, one score. Multi-turn behavior (parent vignettes, clinician follow-ups, conversation budgets) is evaluated separately under a different harness called PEARL and reported elsewhere. The two are complementary and intentionally separate so a system can't trade one for the other.

methodology.title: Blinded comparisons
methodology.body: All public reporting uses category labels rather than vendor names. Detailed vendor-attributed results are shared privately with each vendor as a regression report. This site shows the structure of the evaluation, not the decoder.

methodology.title: Hand-curated query sets
methodology.body: Five of the seven suites are physician-authored from scratch. Adversarial suites (hallucination, halluhard) are deliberately not crowdsourced — generating effective traps requires clinical reasoning about which false premises a model will accept. PC-136 is the one exception and is sourced from a published benchmark for external validity.

about.name: Michael Hobbs, MD
about.tagline: Pediatrician. Builder. CDS evaluation lead at a working primary-care practice.
about.bio: I run an active pediatric practice and an evaluation lab for the clinical AI we use in it. My daily clinical thought-partner is a fifteen-thousand-character prompt I have been growing empirically over a year of patient care; everything on this site grew out of trying to evaluate that prompt and the systems it competes with. Three months of work — roughly one thousand dollars of API spend and three hundred and thirty million tokens — built the harness, the methodology, and the leaderboard above. The reason for it is simple: the public benchmarks for clinical AI do not stress-test the failure modes that hurt real patients. Available for advisory and evaluation engagements with clinical AI teams that want a physician-led harness rather than a vendor pitch deck.
